title: What is the difference between `distinct()` and `dropDuplicates()` in Spark — `distinct()` removes rows where ALL columns match; `dropDuplicates(cols)` removes rows where only the specified columns match (keeps first occurrence) — and when do you use each?

s1_definition.profdef: Both `distinct()` and `dropDuplicates()` remove duplicate rows from a DataFrame, but they differ in which columns define a duplicate. `distinct()` considers a row a duplicate only when every column value matches another row, so it deduplicates on the entire row. `dropDuplicates()` with a subset of columns considers rows duplicates when just those specified columns match, regardless of the other columns, and keeps one occurrence per distinct combination of the subset. Called with no arguments, `dropDuplicates()` behaves like `distinct()`, deduplicating on all columns. You use `distinct()` when exact whole-row duplicates must be removed, and `dropDuplicates(subset)` when a business key — such as a transaction id — defines uniqueness even though other columns may differ.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India imagine a stack of transaction forms. `distinct()` throws away a form only if another form is identical in every single field. `dropDuplicates` on the transaction-id field throws away a form if another form has the same transaction id, even if some other detail like the timestamp or the processing channel differs, keeping just the first one it saw. So if the upstream system re-sent the same transaction twice but stamped a slightly different received-time on the copy, distinct would keep both because they are not fully identical, while dropDuplicates on transaction id would correctly treat them as the same transaction and keep one.
s1_definition.oneliner: distinct() dedupes on all columns (whole-row match); dropDuplicates(subset) dedupes on just the chosen key columns and keeps the first occurrence — use the subset form when a business key defines uniqueness.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Both `distinct()` and `dropDuplicates()` remove duplicate rows from a DataFrame, but they differ in which columns define a duplicate. `distinct()` considers a row a duplicate only when every column value matches another row, so it deduplicates on the entire row. `dropDuplicates()` with a subset of columns considers rows duplicates when just those specified columns match, regardless of the other columns, and keeps one occurrence per distinct combination of the subset. Called with no arguments, `dropDuplicates()` behaves like `distinct()`, deduplicating on all columns. You use `distinct()` when exact whole-row duplicates must be removed, and `dropDuplicates(subset)` when a business key — such as a transaction id — defines uniqueness even though other columns may differ.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India imagine a stack of transaction forms. `distinct()` throws away a form only if another form is identical in every single field. `dropDuplicates` on the transaction-id field throws away a form if another form has the same transaction id, even if some other detail like the timestamp or the processing channel differs, keeping just the first one it saw. So if the upstream system re-sent the same transaction twice but stamped a slightly different received-time on the copy, distinct would keep both because they are not fully identical, while dropDuplicates on transaction id would correctly treat them as the same transaction and keep one.

**One line to remember:** distinct() dedupes on all columns (whole-row match); dropDuplicates(subset) dedupes on just the chosen key columns and keeps the first occurrence — use the subset form when a business key defines uniqueness.

sections.s2_technical:
distinct() removes rows that are identical across every column. Two rows are duplicates only if all their column values are equal, so if any single column differs, both rows are kept. It is a shorthand for deduplicating on the full row and is exactly equivalent to dropDuplicates() called with no column arguments. Use it when you want to collapse genuinely identical records, for example after a union that may have produced exact copies.

dropDuplicates(subset) removes rows that share the same values in the specified subset of columns, ignoring the other columns for the comparison. For each distinct combination of the subset columns, Spark keeps one row and drops the rest. This is the right tool when a subset of columns is the logical key: a transaction id uniquely identifies a transaction even if the row also carries a received-timestamp or a source-channel that varies between duplicate deliveries. You pass the key columns, such as dropDuplicates(["txnId"]), and Spark deduplicates on just those.

A subtle but important point is which row is kept. dropDuplicates on a subset keeps one row per key, but which one is not deterministically specified by the API alone, because it depends on partitioning and ordering. If you need a specific survivor — say the latest by timestamp — you must first order the data or use a window function with row_number to pick the intended row explicitly, rather than relying on dropDuplicates to keep the right one. Treating dropDuplicates as if it keeps the latest is a common bug; it keeps an arbitrary one unless you control ordering.

Both are wide operations that require a shuffle, because determining duplicates across the dataset means bringing rows with matching keys together, so both cost a shuffle similar to a groupBy on the dedup columns. In terms of performance they are comparable; the choice between them is about correctness of the deduplication key, not speed. In Structured Streaming, dropDuplicates is also available and is stateful, remembering seen keys across micro-batches, and there it should be paired with a watermark so the state of remembered keys stays bounded.

A senior-level nuance is choosing the dedup key deliberately and controlling the survivor. In a banking pipeline the business key is almost always a subset — a transaction id, a payment reference, an account-plus-date — not the whole row, because duplicate deliveries differ in metadata like ingestion time. So dropDuplicates on the business key is usually correct and distinct is usually too strict, since distinct would keep both copies whenever any metadata differs. When the surviving row matters, the mature pattern is a window function partitioned by the key and ordered by a tiebreaker, selecting row_number equal to one, which both deduplicates and guarantees the intended survivor. Picking distinct when you meant a subset key, or using dropDuplicates and assuming it keeps the latest, are the two mistakes a senior engineer watches for.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives transactions where the upstream system occasionally re-sends the same transaction with a different received-timestamp. The business key is the transaction id, so dropDuplicates on txnId is correct, while distinct would wrongly keep both because the timestamps differ.

Problem 2 — After unioning two extracts, there may be exact whole-row duplicates that should be collapsed. distinct is the right tool there.

Problem 3 — When deduplicating by transaction id, the bank must keep the latest-received copy, not an arbitrary one, so a window function ordered by timestamp selects the intended survivor.

The demo models a small dataset of transactions with duplicate ids carrying different timestamps, applies distinct, dropDuplicates on txnId, and a window-based latest-wins dedup, logging how many rows each keeps and which survivor the window approach picks.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four rows — T1 on UPI at timestamp 100, T1 on UPI at timestamp 250 (the same transaction re-sent later), T2 on NEFT at 300, and an exact copy of that T2 row.

Step 1: distinct() is applied. It removes only fully identical rows, so the two identical T2 rows collapse into one, but the two T1 rows differ in timestamp and are both kept. The result has three rows: both T1 copies and one T2. This shows distinct is too strict when duplicates differ in metadata.

Step 2: dropDuplicates on txnId is applied. It keeps one row per transaction id, first seen, so T1 collapses to its first copy (timestamp 100) and T2 collapses to one. The result has two rows, correctly treating the re-sent T1 as a single transaction.

Step 3: The latest-wins window dedup is applied. It partitions by txnId and keeps the row with the greatest timestamp, so T1 resolves to the timestamp-250 copy and T2 to one. The result has two rows with the intended survivors, demonstrating deterministic survivor selection.

Step 4: The demo logs all three outcomes, making clear that distinct keeps both T1 copies, dropDuplicates keeps an arbitrary (first) copy, and only the window approach guarantees the latest copy.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:54:00 INFO    distinct() kept 3 rows: [T1/UPI@100, T1/UPI@250, T2/NEFT@300] (T1 copies differ → both kept)
2026-10-30 05:54:00 INFO    dropDuplicates(txnId) kept 2 rows: [T1/UPI@100, T2/NEFT@300] (one per txnId, first seen)
2026-10-30 05:54:00 INFO    latest-wins window kept 2 rows: [T1/UPI@250, T2/NEFT@300] (T1@250 chosen deterministically)
2026-10-30 05:54:00 INFO    Dedup demo complete.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
distinct and dropDuplicates both remove duplicate rows, but they differ in which columns define a duplicate. distinct considers two rows duplicates only when every column matches, so it deduplicates on the whole row and is exactly equivalent to dropDuplicates called with no arguments. dropDuplicates with a subset of columns considers rows duplicates when just those specified columns match, ignoring the others, and keeps one row per distinct combination of the subset. So distinct is strict whole-row deduplication, while dropDuplicates on a subset deduplicates on a chosen business key.

The key practical point in banking is that the business key is almost always a subset, not the whole row. Duplicate deliveries of the same transaction typically differ in metadata like the received timestamp or the source channel, so distinct would wrongly keep both copies because they are not fully identical, whereas dropDuplicates on the transaction id correctly collapses them to one. A subtle trap is that dropDuplicates on a subset keeps an arbitrary surviving row, not necessarily the latest, because which one survives depends on partitioning and ordering. When the surviving row matters, the correct pattern is a window function partitioned by the key and ordered by a tiebreaker like the timestamp, selecting row number one, which both deduplicates and guarantees the intended survivor. Both operations are wide and cost a shuffle similar to a groupBy on the dedup columns, so the choice is about correctness, not speed, and in Structured Streaming dropDuplicates is stateful and must be paired with a watermark to bound the remembered-keys state.

At the National Bank of India our ingestion deduplicated transactions on the transaction id because the upstream system sometimes re-sent the same transaction with a different received-timestamp, and using dropDuplicates on the id was correct where distinct would have kept both copies. Where we needed the latest-received copy for the ledger, we used a window ordered by timestamp with row number one rather than trusting dropDuplicates to keep the right one. The two mistakes I warn about in interviews are choosing distinct when you meant a subset key, which leaves near-duplicates behind, and using dropDuplicates while assuming it keeps the latest, which silently keeps an arbitrary row.
